chapter: Cavalcade, Wynonie Harris and the 1953 show
title: Harris's unpaid tickets, bad language and downfall
summary: Harris lost his home and car, never paid tickets, was banned from broadcasts, and died in California buried by Jimmy Evans.

story.theme_name: Illness, injury and the deaths of colleagues
story.community_name: Illness, injury and death among jazz musicians

blocks.x: And what happened to him ultimately?
To that?
What happened to him in the end?
They had to get rid of him because he wasn't the real boss, but he'd go in there and start pouring whisky and "this is my place" and all that kind of stuff. But what happened, he lost everything.
He did? He lost everything? How?
Well, you see, another thing, he didn't have any driver's license in any state. All the states him because we played a theater in Ohio and

he parked out in a zone where it was no parking on the boulevard right out in front, yes, indeed, and the cop gave him a ticket. And he walked out, saw the ticket, take it, everybody looking at him, tear it up and throw it all in the street, give him another one. He got about 20 tickets like that before he left town. He wouldn't pay any tickets.

So he kept him a chauffeur but then he'd drive, too. And he got those tickets all over the country, and so he was barred from behind the wheel in the United States, a lot of states. He would never pay a ticket. But he'd get them all day.

I was with him in Newark, he'd get him a couple of white girls, blond, and put them in his car. And he's going down to broadcast or do something and in downtown New Jersey, he'd pull right up in the middle of the crossing and turn his car in the wrong way and get out and leave it and go upstairs. The cops would come along, 'whose car is this?' Wymanie on the-ass, you know? Must be Wymanie Harris on the-ass. And that's where he'd get his publicity. He figured if he didn't get it one way he'd get him some blonds (inaudible).

And that's the way he throwed away money, see, and that was his publicity. And he used such bad language all the time. We played Los Angeles, California with this show I had, and I was on the air at the Ballroom for a week, and I was on the air at 8:00. And they had in the

contract, Wymonie Harris wouldn't be allowed in the place till 9:00. All the rest of them could go in the show, and if he come, they'd lock the doors and wouldn't let him in, because he'd come up to the radio and start cussing, see.

Then the last tour I made out there, about ten contracts -- and Benny Carter was out there then. And in the contracts, they had that Wymonie Harris would have to work for straight commission off the door because they wouldn't give him no salary. They didn't want him on the contract. So he went along with that, give him a percentage at the door so if he didn't show up it didn't make no difference.

And he'd come there and say, I ain't working for no salary, I own this thing. And that's what he did the last tour in California, because he may be short, but he raised so much sand like that. But they wouldn't let him broadcast or anything like that on the last tours (inaudible).
Did he just naturally use bad language all the time or was that that an act, too?
(Inaudible.) They had to chase him out of the lot of restaurants. Some filthy language, too. Like, --
When you say he lost everything, --
He lost his home, his car and the end of it, the guys wouldn't pay him no more than $25 a night. And Jimmy ________ would hire him, and they got people paying,
trying to keep his morale up. He used to go with me with the band, and Jimmy Evans would hire him and pay him a little money. (Inaudible.) So he finally got sick, when he so much.
Well, he -- but -- and what did he die of?
I don't know. He was in California.
Oh, he was?
Jimmy Evans went out and buried him because he didn't have any money.
Well, he probably -- he was such an alcoholic.
Yeah, he was sick a long time before that, too.
Yeah. Too bad, because he really did have a lot on the ball, didn't he?
